Fake news

By: Eugene Botha | Production

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
...South Africa is in the grip of a fake news epidemic.

Unique Selling Point:
It is one of the biggest news issues world wide

Summary:
It used be called propaganda in the pre-internet era. Deliberately misleading news reports to promote a certain cause or discredit a certain cause. And mainstream media sponsored by states were mainly used for this. On social media the phenomenon was slower in development but the last 3 years it has exploded. The term Fake News is fairly new and although used by analysts for a couple of years, it really came to the public’s attention during the US election in 2016. Interestingly a lot of the pro-Trump fake news were created in Europe and spread like wildfire over the internet. This was a fairly new development. Initially fake news on the internet was focused on the area of entertainment which is an extension of tabloid news which reported all kinds of made-up stories about celebrities, crime and science. Social media which began incorporating news feeds proved to be pivotal in the development of fake news in the political arena. Fake news now is all over and not always easy to spot. Although the jury is out about how deeply people are influenced by fake new on social media, but it is a significant phenomenon and it seems that South Africa is currently in the grip of a storm of fake news.

Further information:
It used be called propaganda in the pre-internet era. Deliberately misleading news reports to promote a certain cause or discredit a certain cause. And mainstream media sponsored by states were mainly used for this. On social media the phenomenon was slower in development but the last 3 years it has exploded. The term Fake News is fairly new and although used by analysts for a couple of years, it really came to the public’s attention during the US election in 2016. Interestingly a lot of the pro-Trump fake news were created in Europe and spread like wildfire over the internet. This was a fairly new development. Initially fake news on the internet was focused on the area of entertainment which is an extension of tabloid news which reported all kinds of made-up stories about celebrities, crime and science. Social media which began incorporating news feeds proved to be pivotal in the development of fake news in the political arena. Fake news now is all over and not always easy to spot. Although the jury is out about how deeply people are influenced by fake new on social media, but it is a significant phenomenon and it seems that South Africa is currently in the grip of a storm of fake news. This plays itself out in terms of:
• Fake news websites which contains all kinds of false stories – celebrity, political, products. There is a whole bunch fake news websites such as Live Monitor, iMzansi, Mzansi LIVE (“Caster Semenya jets off to Korea for penis transplant”), African News Updates (satirical), Mzansi Stories, News24-TV, CitySun, Gossip Mill Mzansi, Pretorialive, South Africa Latest News. In addition, there is something like typosquatting. TimesLive took the owners of T1meslive to the South African Institute of Intellectual Property Law (SAIIPL) in October last year. In its complaint, TimesLive raised its concern that the T1meslive administrators “might be seeking to damage the TimesLive brand”. SAIIPL found that what was happening there was a form of “typosquatting”, the term for when people deliberately register misspelled domain names in order to drive traffic to their website. In the past, the owners of “standerdbank.co.za”, “sterkinikor.co.za” and “kalula.co.za” have all been slapped down.

• Paid Twitter. This is where people are paid to spread false news. It can also be more benign where the fake news promotes a certain cause or product. But recently it has come to light that it has also been part of the local government elections. A good example of this is the ANC War Room story where it is claimed that the ANC set up a covert operation to try and influence the local government elections in 2016 by spreading fake news. Allegations that its goal was to create posters depicting opposition political parties negatively - were contained in a court application by Sihle Bolani. The public relations strategist fingered Shaka Sisulu, Walter Sisulu’s grandson, as her recruiter, as did Thami Mthimkhulu, a Durban man who has now joined the #PaidTwitter fray. He claimed - on Twitter - that he had been sent slanderous posters to “push” on social media. Another good example is the analysis done last year and published by the Daily Maverick. More than 100 fake Twitter accounts were tracked, all of them advancing three specific narratives; that the State of Capture report was “useless and rubbish”, that the media and Thuli Madonsela were “captured and biased” and that the real enemies of the people were “white monopoly capital” and specifically the Rupert family.

• Fake Twitter accounts of credible news outlets are created accounts to spread misinformation. False accounts have emerged of Talk Radio 702, the Sunday Times, and the Huffington Post, posting false and misleading information, including stories about Finance Minister Pravin Gordhan and others, EWN reported on its website. The tweets appeared to come from established media houses and journalists, but closer inspection revealed subtle changes to their titles, for instance @Radioo702. A good example is the analysis done last year and published by the Daily Maverick. More than 100 fake Twitter accounts were tracked, all of them advancing three specific narratives; that the State of Capture report was “useless and rubbish”, that the media and Thuli Madonsela were “captured and biased” and that the real enemies of the people were “white monopoly capital” and specifically the Rupert family.

• News outlets and individuals are also targeted by fake news. On Saturday 20 January Ferial Haffajee was linked to a tweet purporting to be from the Huffington Post (@HuffingtonPostZA) which said, "Ferial Haffajee: #Gordhan is clearly WMC stooge, going out of his way to clip wings of #Guptas #OakBay". Ferial Haffajee: #Gordhan is clearly WMC stooge, going out of his way to clip wings of #Guptas#OakBay pic.twitter.com/7TdPl3AaCt — HuffPost SouthAfrica (@HuffPostZA) January 20, 2017. A fake City Press website had a picture of a woman sitting on a man's lap. Haffajee’s and business tycoon Johann Rupert's faces are photo-shopped onto the bodies. Haffajee vowed to take on the trolls, which she said started gunning for her in December, after she wrote a column in City Press titled “4 days in December - the year of State Capture”. It seems that Carte Blanche is also the target. A Tweet on 27 January seems to come from a fake twitter account and CB is questioned about non-reporting on ABSA and accused of being part of the “presstitutes”.
In the light of the above we propose a story where we look at the following elements:
• The bigger context - fake news as worldwide phenomenon
• Fake news in South Africa by using 3 examples:
o Paid Twitter (the Sihle Bolani story, the analysis of the 100 fake accounts around the state capture story)
o Websites
o Discrediting Tweets such as the one against Ferial and the one aimed at CB
• We have access to a major social media analysis tool – to analyse the development of a Tweet/term/report to see who it is linked to. We can also use the tool to find out who is behind is behind fake news websites and trace the owners.
• Who is supposed to control/police this?
• Fake news is going to get even worse: we will include some guidelines on how to spot fake news.

Possible interviewees: tobe decided
• Arthur Goldstruck -- WorldWideWorx
• William Bird – Media Monitoring Africa
• Ferial Hafferjee
• Xolani Dube Xubera Institute for Research and Development, Durban
• Somebody from South African National Editors’ Forum (SANEF)
• Peter Fryer – digital forensic expert



Extra Budget Items:
Xolani Dube is in Durban

Expert:
Mr. Peter Fryer
Mr. William Bird
Ms. Ferial Haffajee
Mr. Xolani Dube
Ms. Graig Raw Lauren Green

Locations:
Gauteng and Durban

Script:


Xolani:
We live in a post-truth era where lies are the new normal.
V/O:
Xolani Dube is a researcher at the Xubera Research Institute in Kwazulu Natal an organization analysing South African society. The lies he is referring to are present in the so-called fake news stories found all over social media. And if used to further political aims, it becomes very serious business.
19
Xolani:
It is a war. It is an information war.
V/O:
William Bird, CEO of news monitoring agency Media Monitoring Africa, says fake news is created deliberately for two purposes.
9
William:
Fake news is material that presents itself as news but it is either put out in order to make money, so it is used as click-bait type stuff or it is put out to deliberately misinform people.
V/O:
This is click-bait: stories that are designed to entice people to click on them. Every click generates money for the creators. These websites are notoriously difficult to recognize because they appear legitimate, but mix fake news in with actual news.
18
Peter:
The fake news sites are presented as actual news sites and I think a recent study conducted by Stanford University shows that 82% or people surveyed cannot tell the difference between real news sites and fake news sites.
V/O:
Peter Fryer is a digital forensic expert and he says there are literally dozens of fake news websites in South Africa.

Live Monitor iMzansi Mzansi LIVE African News Updates Mzansi Stories News24-TV
CitySun Gossip Mill Mzansi Pretorialive South Africa Latest News

The websites spewing fake news usually try to conceal exactly who is behind them. We asked Peter to see if he could identify the masterminds driving some of the sites.

This is mzansilive.co.za and it looks like an ordinary website. But this is the lead story -- apparently South Africa is going to build a wall to keep Zimbabweans out.

Who is behind this kind of fake news?
8






7 +5


10

4
Peter:
So we have had to dig a bit deeper using other techniques that are not exactly in the domain of the average person using the internet.
V/O:
When Peter analysed the MzansiLIVE website he found that it linked to several other news websites – SABC1news.co.za, africalive24.com, africa24live.com and Pretorialive.co.za. They were all registered by an Etinos Mudzamba, with an address in Zimbabwe.

Peter:
So this would be the person that has registered the website. This is the information that is linked back to that website.

Nobody at the Harare number knew anything about websites and when Peter looked up Etinos on Facebook he found this picture. However, the same photograph is also used for a Jonathan Si/mango and a Ta/tenda Machi/ven/yika. These are fake identities. We found much the same with other websites: it is virtually impossible to find out who is creating the fake news and why. Is it just money or something more sinister?

The term “Fake News” became a house-hold expression in the run-up to and after the US election.

20






26





Tump:
…. I saw the information, I read the information outside of that meeting. It's all fake news. It's phony stuff. It did not happen. You are fake news.
V/O:
Trump now complains about fake news but during the election campaign his supporters used fake news to vilify his opponent.
7
Hillary:
The epidemic of malicious fake news and false propaganda that flooded social media over the past year, it's now clear that so-called fake news can have real world consequences.
V/O:
And the real world consequences for Clinton were losing the election.

Craig Raw is the founder of BrandsEye, a company specializing in analysing social media and its impact.
4

6
Devi Question:
In your mind do you think fake news was a prominent source of information in terms of the US election?
Craig:
There's certainly a great deal of evidence to show that fake news was widely spread. There was a great deal of smearing around Hillary Clinton and I think that even now you will find that the perception of her is in a different place to where it was even if people knew that much of that news was fake.
V/O:
Ferial Haffajee editor-at-large of the Huffington Post South Africa says that in the last year political fake news has become part of social media in this country. And Twitter is in/tegral to this.
12
Ferial:
Twitter is now the most influential form of social media in South Africa. It used to be Carte Blanche, Sunday Times, and City Press etc. Now it is social media and of the social media it is Twitter.
V/O:
There’s lots of fake news on Twitter and Facebook is not far behind.
6
Xolani:
Facebook is no longer innocent. It has become a powerful tool for power as well as a serious transmitter of propaganda and untruthfulness.
V/O:
We approached both Facebook and Twitter for comments on how they are tackling the issue of fake news but they declined to participate.

Because Twitter accounts can be set up anonymously it makes them ideal for spreading fake news. In December last year Ferial bore the brunt of a malicious Twitter fake news campaign. It started after she published a piece about State Capture by the Gupta family.
8



18

Ferial:
The next day I started getting these fake troll accounts, images of me saying things that I would never say, making allegations about me.
V/O:
These are some of the malicious Tweets about Ferial……. She is falsely accused of being a puppet of white monopoly capital. They were Tweeted and re-Tweeted thousands of times in December.
12
Ferial:
I felt violated by it.

Devi:
It does something to you that is hard to explain… yes, yes …..
V/O:
On the 20th of January this year there was another upsurge in these sort of Tweets. Craig introduced us to one of his analysts, Lauren Green, who researched the accounts tweeting about Ferial and other journalists.


Lauren:
So the way we noticed that suddenly there were four accounts titled Huffington Post SA, Sunday Times, Radio 702 and the Daily Maverick. There were slight misspellings in some of the handles.

Devi:
Slight?

Lauren:
Yes very slight. But the profile pictures in them made them look almost like the real thing. So using those four accounts I found an overlap of 225 authors that re-tweeted the content of every single one of those accounts.
V/O:
So the four fake accounts all started to spew fake news on the 20th of January. Then 225 other accounts retweeted the content in unison on the same day. All the tweets were negative towards Pravin Gordhan and the State Capture Report and favourable towards the Gupta family. All in all the 225 fake accounts sent out a staggering 87 000 fake news Tweets.

It was part of an orchestrated campaign to influence public opinion.

Every time we open Facebook we are confronted by fake news.

26



LINK:
But is there a way to spot fake news?
V/O:
We gathered the following advice
• Cross-check news stories against reputable news sources
• Be very critical about what you read on-line
• Investigate the web address and domain name
• Many shares do not mean the story is true

Fake news can be really dangerous because political misinformation and vilification of individuals can leave people uncertain about what is truth and lies when it comes to making decisions about the world, their lives and politics.







14
William:
The moment we undermine people’s ability to make informed choices we undermine very clearly and directly your democracy. It is that simple.

Craig Raw is the founder of BrandsEye, a company specializing in analysing social media and its impact. 4 6 Devi Question: In your mind do you think fake news was a prominent source of information in terms of the US election? Craig: There's certainly a great deal of evidence to show that fake news was widely spread. There was a great deal of smearing around Hillary Clinton and I think that even now you will find that the perception of her is in a different place to where it was even if people knew that much of that news was fake. V/O: Ferial Haffajee editor-at-large of the Huffington Post South Africa says that in the last year political fake news has become part of social media in this country. And Twitter is in/tegral to this. 12 Ferial: Twitter is now the most influential form of social media in South Africa. It used to be Carte Blanche, Sunday Times, and City Press etc. Now it is social media and of the social media it is Twitter. V/O: There’s lots of fake news on Twitter and Facebook is not far behind. 6 Xolani: Facebook is no longer innocent. It has become a powerful tool for power as well as a serious transmitter of propaganda and untruthfulness. V/O: We approached both Facebook and Twitter for comments on how they are tackling the issue of fake news but they declined to participate. Because Twitter accounts can be set up anonymously it makes them ideal for spreading fake news. In December last year Ferial bore the brunt of a malicious Twitter fake news campaign. It started after she published a piece about State Capture by the Gupta family. 8 18 Ferial: The next day I started getting these fake troll accounts, images of me saying things that I would never say, making allegations about me. V/O: These are some of the malicious Tweets about Ferial……. She is falsely accused of being a puppet of white monopoly capital. They were Tweeted and re-Tweeted thousands of times in December. 12 Ferial: I felt violated by it. Devi: It does something to you that is hard to explain… yes, yes ….. V/O: On the 20th of January this year there was another upsurge in these sort of Tweets. Craig introduced us to one of his analysts, Lauren Green, who researched the accounts tweeting about Ferial and other journalists. Lauren: So the way we noticed that suddenly there were four accounts titled Huffington Post SA, Sunday Times, Radio 702 and the Daily Maverick. There were slight misspellings in some of the handles. Devi: Slight? Lauren: Yes very slight. But the profile pictures in them made them look almost like the real thing. So using those four accounts I found an overlap of 225 authors that re-tweeted the content of every single one of those accounts. V/O: So the four fake accounts all started to spew fake news on the 20th of January. Then 225 other accounts retweeted the content in unison on the same day. All the tweets were negative towards Pravin Gordhan and the State Capture Report and favourable towards the Gupta family. All in all the 225 fake accounts sent out a staggering 87 000 fake news Tweets. It was part of an orchestrated campaign to influence public opinion. Every time we open Facebook we are confronted by fake news. 26 LINK: But is there a way to spot fake news? V/O: We gathered the following advice • Cross-check news stories against reputable news sources • Be very critical about what you read on-line • Investigate the web address and domain name • Many shares do not mean the story is true Fake news can be really dangerous because political misinformation and vilification of individuals can leave people uncertain about what is truth and lies when it comes to making decisions about the world, their lives and politics. 14 William: The moment we undermine people’s ability to make informed choices we undermine very clearly and directly your democracy. It is that simple.

metadata.Summary: It used be called propaganda in the pre-internet era. Deliberately misleading news reports to promote a certain cause or discredit a certain cause. And mainstream media sponsored by states were mainly used for this. On social media the phenomenon was slower in development but the last 3 years it has exploded. The term Fake News is fairly new and although used by analysts for a couple of years, it really came to the public’s attention during the US election in 2016. Interestingly a lot of the pro-Trump fake news were created in Europe and spread like wildfire over the internet. This was a fairly new development. Initially fake news on the internet was focused on the area of entertainment which is an extension of tabloid news which reported all kinds of made-up stories about celebrities, crime and science. Social media which began incorporating news feeds proved to be pivotal in the development of fake news in the political arena. Fake news now is all over and not always easy to spot. Although the jury is out about how deeply people are influenced by fake new on social media, but it is a significant phenomenon and it seems that South Africa is currently in the grip of a storm of fake news.
metadata.Further information: It used be called propaganda in the pre-internet era. Deliberately misleading news reports to promote a certain cause or discredit a certain cause. And mainstream media sponsored by states were mainly used for this. On social media the phenomenon was slower in development but the last 3 years it has exploded. The term Fake News is fairly new and although used by analysts for a couple of years, it really came to the public’s attention during the US election in 2016. Interestingly a lot of the pro-Trump fake news were created in Europe and spread like wildfire over the internet. This was a fairly new development. Initially fake news on the internet was focused on the area of entertainment which is an extension of tabloid news which reported all kinds of made-up stories about celebrities, crime and science. Social media which began incorporating news feeds proved to be pivotal in the development of fake news in the political arena. Fake news now is all over and not always easy to spot. Although the jury is out about how deeply people are influenced by fake new on social media, but it is a significant phenomenon and it seems that South Africa is currently in the grip of a storm of fake news. This plays itself out in terms of: • Fake news websites which contains all kinds of false stories – celebrity, political, products. There is a whole bunch fake news websites such as Live Monitor, iMzansi, Mzansi LIVE (“Caster Semenya jets off to Korea for penis transplant”), African News Updates (satirical), Mzansi Stories, News24-TV, CitySun, Gossip Mill Mzansi, Pretorialive, South Africa Latest News. In addition, there is something like typosquatting. TimesLive took the owners of T1meslive to the South African Institute of Intellectual Property Law (SAIIPL) in October last year. In its complaint, TimesLive raised its concern that the T1meslive administrators “might be seeking to damage the TimesLive brand”. SAIIPL found that what was happening there was a form of “typosquatting”, the term for when people deliberately register misspelled domain names in order to drive traffic to their website. In the past, the owners of “standerdbank.co.za”, “sterkinikor.co.za” and “kalula.co.za” have all been slapped down. • Paid Twitter. This is where people are paid to spread false news. It can also be more benign where the fake news promotes a certain cause or product. But recently it has come to light that it has also been part of the local government elections. A good example of this is the ANC War Room story where it is claimed that the ANC set up a covert operation to try and influence the local government elections in 2016 by spreading fake news. Allegations that its goal was to create posters depicting opposition political parties negatively - were contained in a court application by Sihle Bolani. The public relations strategist fingered Shaka Sisulu, Walter Sisulu’s grandson, as her recruiter, as did Thami Mthimkhulu, a Durban man who has now joined the #PaidTwitter fray. He claimed - on Twitter - that he had been sent slanderous posters to “push” on social media. Another good example is the analysis done last year and published by the Daily Maverick. More than 100 fake Twitter accounts were tracked, all of them advancing three specific narratives; that the State of Capture report was “useless and rubbish”, that the media and Thuli Madonsela were “captured and biased” and that the real enemies of the people were “white monopoly capital” and specifically the Rupert family. • Fake Twitter accounts of credible news outlets are created accounts to spread misinformation. False accounts have emerged of Talk Radio 702, the Sunday Times, and the Huffington Post, posting false and misleading information, including stories about Finance Minister Pravin Gordhan and others, EWN reported on its website. The tweets appeared to come from established media houses and journalists, but closer inspection revealed subtle changes to their titles, for instance @Radioo702. A good example is the analysis done last year and published by the Daily Maverick. More than 100 fake Twitter accounts were tracked, all of them advancing three specific narratives; that the State of Capture report was “useless and rubbish”, that the media and Thuli Madonsela were “captured and biased” and that the real enemies of the people were “white monopoly capital” and specifically the Rupert family. • News outlets and individuals are also targeted by fake news. On Saturday 20 January Ferial Haffajee was linked to a tweet purporting to be from the Huffington Post (@HuffingtonPostZA) which said, "Ferial Haffajee: #Gordhan is clearly WMC stooge, going out of his way to clip wings of #Guptas #OakBay". Ferial Haffajee: #Gordhan is clearly WMC stooge, going out of his way to clip wings of #Guptas#OakBay pic.twitter.com/7TdPl3AaCt — HuffPost SouthAfrica (@HuffPostZA) January 20, 2017. A fake City Press website had a picture of a woman sitting on a man's lap. Haffajee’s and business tycoon Johann Rupert's faces are photo-shopped onto the bodies. Haffajee vowed to take on the trolls, which she said started gunning for her in December, after she wrote a column in City Press titled “4 days in December - the year of State Capture”. It seems that Carte Blanche is also the target. A Tweet on 27 January seems to come from a fake twitter account and CB is questioned about non-reporting on ABSA and accused of being part of the “presstitutes”. In the light of the above we propose a story where we look at the following elements: • The bigger context - fake news as worldwide phenomenon • Fake news in South Africa by using 3 examples: o Paid Twitter (the Sihle Bolani story, the analysis of the 100 fake accounts around the state capture story) o Websites o Discrediting Tweets such as the one against Ferial and the one aimed at CB • We have access to a major social media analysis tool – to analyse the development of a Tweet/term/report to see who it is linked to. We can also use the tool to find out who is behind is behind fake news websites and trace the owners. • Who is supposed to control/police this? • Fake news is going to get even worse: we will include some guidelines on how to spot fake news.
